rows.subtopic: Factors Influencing Rate of a Reaction
rows.stem: A reaction is of second order with respect to a reactant. How is the rate of reaction affected if the concentration of the reactant is (i) doubled (ii) reduced to half ?
rows.solution:
Second order in the reactant means rate \(= k[\mathrm{R}]^2\), so the rate changes as the SQUARE of the concentration.

(i) Doubling the concentration:
\(\text{new rate} = k(2[\mathrm{R}])^2 = 4\,k[\mathrm{R}]^2\)
The rate becomes 4 times what it was.

(ii) Halving the concentration:
\(\text{new rate} = k\left(\dfrac{[\mathrm{R}]}{2}\right)^2 = \dfrac{1}{4}k[\mathrm{R}]^2\)
The rate falls to one quarter of what it was.

rows.subtopic: Some Important Compounds of Transition Elements
rows.stem: When \(\mathrm{FeCr_2O_4}\) is fused with \(\mathrm{Na_2CO_3}\) in the presence of air it gives a yellow solution of compound (A). Compound (A) on acidification gives compound (B). Compound (B) on reaction with \(\mathrm{KCl}\) forms an orange coloured (C). An acidified solution of compound (C) oxidises \(\mathrm{Na_2SO_3}\) to (D). Identify (A), (B), (C) and (D).
rows.solution:
This is the industrial route from chromite ore to potassium dichromate, and the colours named in the question are the clues.

Fusing chromite with sodium carbonate in air oxidises chromium from \(+3\) to \(+6\), giving the YELLOW chromate:
\(4\mathrm{FeCr_2O_4} + 8\mathrm{Na_2CO_3} + 7\mathrm{O_2} \longrightarrow 8\mathrm{Na_2CrO_4} + 2\mathrm{Fe_2O_3} + 8\mathrm{CO_2}\)
\(\mathrm{A} = \mathrm{Na_2CrO_4}\), sodium chromate

Acidification converts chromate to dichromate, chromium staying at \(+6\):
\(\mathrm{B} = \mathrm{Na_2Cr_2O_7}\), sodium dichromate

Potassium chloride exchanges the cation and the much less soluble potassium salt crystallises out ORANGE:
\(\mathrm{C} = \mathrm{K_2Cr_2O_7}\), potassium dichromate

Acidified dichromate is a strong oxidising agent and takes sulphite, in which sulphur is \(+4\), to sulphate, in which it is \(+6\):
\(\mathrm{Cr_2O_7^{2-}} + 3\mathrm{SO_3^{2-}} + 8\mathrm{H^+} \longrightarrow 2\mathrm{Cr^{3+}} + 3\mathrm{SO_4^{2-}} + 4\mathrm{H_2O}\)
\(\mathrm{D} = \mathrm{Na_2SO_4}\), sodium sulphate

rows.stem: Explain \(\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_6]^{3+}}\) is an inner orbital complex whereas \(\mathrm{[Ni(NH_3)_6]^{2+}}\) is an outer orbital complex. [At. No. Co = 27, Ni = 28]
rows.solution:
Both complexes have six ammine ligands, so the ligand is not what separates them — the number of d electrons is.

In \(\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_6]^{3+}}\) cobalt is \(+3\), so \(\mathrm{Co^{3+}}\) is \(3d^6\). Ammonia is a strong enough field ligand to pair those six electrons, and six electrons fill exactly three orbitals, leaving TWO \(3d\) orbitals empty. Two is precisely what \(d^2sp^3\) hybridisation needs, so the inner \(3d\) orbitals are used and the complex is an INNER ORBITAL complex.

In \(\mathrm{[Ni(NH_3)_6]^{2+}}\) nickel is \(+2\), so \(\mathrm{Ni^{2+}}\) is \(3d^8\). Even if every electron paired, eight electrons fill four orbitals and leave only ONE \(3d\) orbital free — and one is not enough. The bonding must therefore use outer \(4d\) orbitals, giving \(sp^3d^2\) and an OUTER ORBITAL complex.

The deciding factor is simply whether two inner d orbitals can be vacated, and for \(d^8\) they cannot.

rows.stem:
Calculate \(\Lambda^{\circ}\mathrm{m}\) for acetic acid and its degree of dissociation \((\alpha)\) if its molar conductivity is 48.1 \(\Omega^{-1}\ \mathrm{cm^2\ mol^{-1}}\).
Given that
\(\Lambda^{\circ}\mathrm{m}\ \mathrm{(HCl)} = 426\ \Omega^{-1}\ \mathrm{cm^2\ mol^{-1}}\)
\(\Lambda^{\circ}\mathrm{m}\ \mathrm{(NaCl)} = 126\ \Omega^{-1}\ \mathrm{cm^2\ mol^{-1}}\)
\(\Lambda^{\circ}\mathrm{m}\ \mathrm{(CH_3COONa)} = 91\ \Omega^{-1}\ \mathrm{cm^2\ mol^{-1}}\)
rows.solution:
Acetic acid is a weak electrolyte, so its limiting molar conductivity cannot be found by extrapolation and must be built up from strong electrolytes by Kohlrausch's law. Choose three whose ions combine to give acetic acid's:
\(\Lambda^{\circ}_m(\mathrm{CH_3COOH}) = \Lambda^{\circ}_m(\mathrm{HCl}) + \Lambda^{\circ}_m(\mathrm{CH_3COONa}) - \Lambda^{\circ}_m(\mathrm{NaCl})\)

The bookkeeping works because the first two supply \(\mathrm{H^+} + \mathrm{Cl^-}\) and \(\mathrm{CH_3COO^-} + \mathrm{Na^+}\), and subtracting the third removes the \(\mathrm{Na^+}\) and \(\mathrm{Cl^-}\), leaving exactly \(\mathrm{H^+} + \mathrm{CH_3COO^-}\).

\(\Lambda^{\circ}_m = 426 + 91 - 126 = 391\ \Omega^{-1}\ \mathrm{cm^2\ mol^{-1}}\)

The degree of dissociation is the ratio of the measured molar conductivity to that limiting value:
\(\alpha = \dfrac{\Lambda_m}{\Lambda^{\circ}_m} = \dfrac{48.1}{391} = 0.123\)

So about 12% of the acid is dissociated at this concentration.

rows.subtopic: General Properties of the Transition Elements (d-Block)
rows.stem:
(a) Of the \(\mathrm{d^4}\) species, \(\mathrm{Cr^{2+}}\) is strongly reducing while \(\mathrm{Mn^{3+}}\) is strongly oxidising. Why ?
(b) Write two consequences of lanthanoid contraction.
(c) Which element of 3d series has lowest enthalpy of atomisation and why ?
rows.solution:
(a) Both are \(d^4\) species, and in each case it is the STABILITY OF THE ION THEY BECOME that drives the behaviour. \(\mathrm{Cr^{2+}}\) is strongly reducing because losing one more electron gives \(\mathrm{Cr^{3+}}\), which is \(3d^3\) — a half-filled \(t_{2g}\) set, a specially stable arrangement — so the chromium gives up that electron readily. \(\mathrm{Mn^{3+}}\) is strongly oxidising because GAINING one electron gives \(\mathrm{Mn^{2+}}\), which is \(3d^5\), an exactly half-filled d subshell, equally stable — so the manganese takes an electron readily.

(b) Two consequences. First, the elements of the 4d and 5d series have almost the same atomic radii — zirconium and hafnium, niobium and tantalum — because the contraction across the lanthanoids cancels the expected increase; this makes those pairs very hard to separate. Second, the lanthanoids themselves become progressively harder to separate from one another, since their ionic radii shrink so gradually that their chemical properties are nearly identical.

(c) Zinc has the lowest enthalpy of atomisation in the 3d series. Enthalpy of atomisation measures the strength of the metallic bonding, which depends on the number of unpaired d electrons an atom contributes. Zinc is \(3d^{10} 4s^2\): its d subshell is completely filled and its \(4s\) electrons are paired, so no unpaired electron is available for interatomic bonding. The metallic bond is correspondingly weak, and zinc is also the lowest-melting metal of the series.

rows.stem:
Write IUPAC names of the following coordination entities :
(a) \(\mathrm{[Fe(en)_2Cl_2]^{+}}\)
(b) \(\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_4(H_2O)Br]SO_4}\)
(c) \(\mathrm{[Ni\,(CN)_4]^{2-}}\)
rows.solution:
(a) The ion carries \(+1\). Inside it the two ethane-1,2-diamine ligands are neutral and the two chlorido ligands contribute \(-1\) each, so iron is \(+3\). Chlorido precedes ethane-1,2-diamine alphabetically, and the latter takes bis because its name contains numerals:
dichloridobis(ethane-1,2-diamine)iron(III) ion

(b) The sulphate ion outside carries \(-2\), so the complex cation is \(+2\). Inside it the bromido ligand is \(-1\) and the four ammine and one aqua ligand are neutral, so cobalt is \(+3\). Alphabetical order gives ammine, aqua, bromido:
tetraammineaquabromidocobalt(III) sulphate

(c) Four cyanido ligands contribute \(-4\) against an overall \(-2\), so nickel is \(+2\). The species is an anion, so nickel takes the \(-ate\) ending:
tetracyanidonickelate(II) ion

rows.stem:
(a) Write the product obtained when D-glucose reacts with \(\mathrm{H_2N-OH}\).
(b) Amino acids show amphoteric behaviour, why ?
(c) Why vitamin C cannot be stored in our body ?
rows.solution:
(a) Hydroxylamine condenses with the free aldehyde group at C-1, losing water, to give glucose oxime:
\(\mathrm{CHO(CHOH)_4CH_2OH} + \mathrm{H_2N-OH} \longrightarrow \mathrm{CH{=}N-OH(CHOH)_4CH_2OH} + \mathrm{H_2O}\)
This is one of the reactions establishing that a carbonyl group is present in the open chain form.

(b) Because an amino acid exists as a ZWITTERION. Its \(-\mathrm{COOH}\) group transfers its proton to its own \(-\mathrm{NH_2}\) group, giving \(\mathrm{H_3\overset{+}{N}-CHR-COO^-}\), which carries both an acidic and a basic centre. In the presence of a base the \(-\mathrm{\overset{+}{N}H_3}\) group gives up a proton, so the amino acid acts as an acid; in the presence of an acid the \(-\mathrm{COO^-}\) group accepts one, so it acts as a base. Having both functional groups in one molecule is what makes the behaviour amphoteric.

(c) Vitamin C is WATER soluble. Water-soluble vitamins cannot be stored: any amount beyond immediate need dissolves in the body fluids and is excreted in the urine. Vitamin C must therefore be supplied regularly in the diet, unlike the fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E and K, which are stored in the liver and in adipose tissue.
